course_name_original: CORE- Antropología II, Grupo A, B, C (TECNUN) (antropologia2ing)
course_name_en: CORE- Anthropology II, Group A, B, C (TECNUN)

learning_outcomes.text: Promote the development of personality in all its dimensions: scientific, cultural, human, etc.; so that it translates into a greater development of critical capacity and a knowledge of problems, leading to an exercise of freedom that, respecting legitimate pluralism, is sensitive to manifestations of solidarity and fraternity and helps to build spaces of equality, coexistence and friendship.
Promote the social values typical of a peaceful culture, contributing to democratic coexistence, respect for Human Rights and fundamental principles such as equality and non-discrimination.
Understand that the university spirit critically and reflectively approaches the study of the discipline and its connection with other knowledge.
Identify the most relevant questions of human existence and adopt a reasoned personal stance towards them.
Discover and judge the anthropological assumptions and ethical repercussions of one's own discipline.

That students have demonstrated possession and understanding of knowledge in a field of study that builds on general secondary education, and is typically found at a level that, while supported by advanced textbooks, also includes some aspects that involve knowledge from the forefront of their field of study.
Apply knowledge to work professionally, develop and defend arguments, and solve problems within their field of study.
That students have the ability to gather and interpret relevant data to make prudent judgments.
That students can transmit information, ideas, problems and solutions to diverse audiences (specialized and non-specialized).
Learn to identify the most relevant questions of human existence and adopt a reasoned personal stance towards them.
Discover and judge the anthropological assumptions and ethical repercussions of one's own actions, and of professional performance.
Value the dignity of each person, and one's own.

syllabus_topics: Philosophical anthropology or Philosophy of the human being
Different views and problems of anthropology.
"Can a subject be, at the same time, subject and object of a science?"
Singularity of the human being. Notion of nature.
Is the human being composite, or is it just matter?
Theme II. The living human being in time and space.
The structure of reality. Life and the inert. Introduction
Characteristics of the living: unity, organicity.
Action of the living: self-movement, immanence
Levels of life. Basic vital operations.
The soul. Pythagoras. Plato. Aristotle. Language.
The human being in space and time. The three areas: biosphere, polis, cyberspace
Theme III: The personal identity of the human being.
What is human identity? Definition. Etymology of the word identity. Understanding the definition of identity.
Discovering and building one's own identity. Components of identity
Components. Origin. Memory. Self-knowledge and acceptance. Relationship with others. Dynamic identity.
Achieving an authentic personal identity. Foundation.
Human identity: Is there something common to all human beings?
Theme IV: Knowledge, intelligence, and language. The human mind.
Memory and thought. Memory and identity.
What is language. Types of language.
Can intelligence increase? Ideas about transhumanism.
Operations of human thinking. Abstraction. Judgment. Reasoning.
Thought and language. Influence of feelings on language.
What is the thinking like? Reflective, immaterial, self-awareness.
What is freedom. Definition of freedom.
The realization of freedom. The vital project.
Theme VI. The personality. Temperament and character. The emotions. The affectivity.
Theme VII. The virtues, fullness of freedom.
Growth in virtue according to Aristotle.
The formation of the person. The ideal of excellence.
Theme VIII. The human being. Biology and sex.
The human body and the body of animals.
Different philosophical conceptions about the human body.
The human body as a part of the person.
Integration of the levels of sexuality.
The gift of the body in eros.
The integration of body and reason. Human behavior.
Theme IX. The human person. Greatness and dignity. The Consciens.
The dignity of the person, the foundation of ethics.
The anthropological foundation of the person.
Ethics is based on the concept of person
The person is whole and part at the same time
Etymology and definition of the word person
Reflections on the term person. Consequences.
Need to recover the idea and concept of person
The human person. Animals and computers.
Why do we say we have spirit. Characters of the spirit.
Respect for others, respect to the others.
assessment_rules: The ordinary call assessment will be based on two paper-based multiple-choice exams, one mid-semester and one at the end, each contributing 50% to the grade. The extraordinary call will consist of a single paper-based multiple-choice exam.
